correctness.rationale: In a terminal two-coloring, a color class missing both universal vertices dominates only if it equals all of the independent part. Hence Alice wins exactly when the two universal vertices have different colors, or when they have the same color and every independent vertex has the opposite color. The four parity/starting-player strategies in the proof are exhaustive pairing strategies: the player controlling the universal pair can force opposite colors in the winning parity and Bob can force equal universal colors plus a mixed independent part in the losing parity. Hartnell--Rall's even-minimum-degree bound gives the global palette upper bound two because \(\delta=2\), while one color is trivially winnable. The ordinary partition \(\{u\},\{v\},W\) gives domatic number three and \(\delta+1\) is the matching upper bound. The packaged exact minimax verifier was read and independently confirms both starting conventions through \(n=7\); the infinite proof is the pairing argument.
correctness.risk: The result is confined to the one-parameter split/complete-tripartite family.

value.rationale: The family is the simplest non-bipartite complete-multipartite extension of the complete-bipartite benchmark, and it cleanly isolates a starting-player effect: the two game values swap with parity while the ordinary domatic number remains three. That is a motivated infinite game-theoretic classification rather than a small computational table.
value.risk: No claim is made for general complete multipartite or split graphs.

final_claim: For \(G_n=K_{1,1,n}\) with \(n\ge2\), Alice-start game domatic number is \(2\) for odd \(n\) and \(1\) for even \(n\), while Bob-start has the reversed parity values; the ordinary domatic number is always \(3\).
limitations: Finite minimax checks are stress tests rather than the proof.
